prompt.brief: Design an IDE and CI-integrated code assistant that serves low-latency completions, code generation, explanations, and review while protecting source code and respecting repository context.
successSignals: Define editor context boundaries, repository indexing, language parsing, prompt construction, completion cancellation, model versions, and telemetry consent.
Keep inline completion bounded and fast while supporting multi-file retrieval, workspace isolation, secret/PII redaction, and context freshness.
Separate interactive inference from indexing, batch code review, evaluation, and CI workflows; make requests cancellable and retries safe.
Explain hallucination/security risks, licensing, prompt injection, data retention, rollout, observability, and a local/cache fallback.

functional: Provide inline and chat completions, natural-language code generation, explanations, refactoring, test generation, review comments, and CI annotations.
Index authorized repositories with branch/version awareness, retrieve relevant context, stream/cancel responses, and show model/context metadata.
Support tenant policies, repository deletion, telemetry opt-out, rate limits, model rollback, prompt-injection defenses, and dependency failure.
nonFunctional: Meet p95 first-token inline completion latency under 200ms for warm contexts and cap context retrieval/inference work.
Scale to 1M active developers and large repository indexes without a single hot key or unbounded synchronous work.
Do not lose committed state; make retries and duplicate events safe.
Degrade safely when downstream workers, caches, or external dependencies fail.
scaleAssumptions: 1M developers, 100k concurrent IDE sessions, and million-file repositories
Partition by the primary tenant, user, item, or geographic key and isolate hot partitions.
Keep serving state bounded; retain raw events or durable records for replay and auditing.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the IDE commit authoritative; let derived projections converge with visible version and freshness.
Use idempotency keys, conditional IDE writes, event IDs, and versions so retries and replay are safe.
Return IDE version and observedAt so clients can reason about freshness.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition IDE by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound IDE work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for IDE projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable IDE projection or an explicit degraded response when workers fail.
Retain durable IDE records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure IDE latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.
